prompt: Write a vivid opening paragraph for a mystery set on a night train.
task_completions: The Orient Star was a velvet coffin gliding through the inky Polish countryside. Rain lashed against the panoramic windows, blurring the fleeting glimpses of frosted fields and skeletal trees into an impressionistic smear of grey and black. Inside, the air hung thick with the scent of coal smoke, stale perfume, and a quiet desperation only a long journey can breed. I’d barely settled into my compartment – a plush, burgundy-walled space that felt both opulent and claustrophobic – when the scream cut through the rhythmic clatter of the wheels, a high, thin wail that instantly silenced the murmur of conversation and promised a night far removed from peaceful transit. It wasn't the scream of fear, though. It was the scream of *discovery*. And I had a terrible feeling whatever had been discovered, was now very, very dead.

The Orient Star was a velvet coffin gliding through the inky Polish countryside. Rain lashed against the panoramic windows, blurring the skeletal trees into streaks of black, and the rhythmic clatter of the wheels was a hypnotic pulse against the low hum of conversation and the clinking of crystal in the dining car. But beneath the veneer of luxurious travel, a disquiet had settled. It wasn’t the usual train restlessness, the shifting anxieties of strangers thrown together in close quarters. This was colder, sharper – a prickling on the back of the neck that had nothing to do with the draft from a poorly sealed window, and everything to do with the fact that, just an hour ago, the renowned art collector, Mr. Silas Blackwood, had been found slumped in his compartment, a single crimson stain blooming on the pristine white linen of his travelling suit. And the door had been locked from the inside.

The Orient Star was a velvet coffin rolling through the inky Polish countryside. Rain lashed against the panoramic windows, blurring the fleeting glimpses of frosted fields and skeletal trees into an impressionistic smear of grey and black. Inside, a hushed opulence reigned – plush crimson seats, the clink of crystal glasses from the dining car, the low murmur of languages I didn’t recognize. But beneath the veneer of luxury, a current of unease prickled my skin. It wasn’t the storm, or the rhythmic clatter of the wheels on the tracks, but the way Madame Evangeline Rostova, a woman draped in more pearls than sense, had stared at me across the smoky lounge car, her eyes holding a desperate, silent plea just moments before she excused herself… and vanished. Now, only an empty chair and the lingering scent of her expensive perfume remained, and a feeling, cold and sharp as the November wind, told me she hadn't simply gone to her cabin.
